questions.title: Why does the sequence-level importance ratio $s_i(\theta)$ include a $1/|y_i|$ exponent?
questions.question_body: In the GSPO algorithm section, the importance ratio is defined as $s_{i}(\theta) = \left( \frac{ \pi_{\theta} (y_i | x) }{ \pi_{\theta_\text{old}} (y_i | x)} \right)^{\frac{1}{|y_i|}}$. I understand that $\pi_{\theta} (y_i | x)$ is the product of token probabilities, which gets extremely small for long sequences. However, why do we take the geometric mean (via the $1/|y_i|$ exponent) instead of just using the raw sequence likelihood ratio? Is this purely to prevent numerical underflow, or does it serve a specific purpose in controlling the variance of the estimator relative to sequence length?

questions.title: How exactly does 'expert-activation volatility' invalidate token-level importance weights in MoE models?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions that for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models trained with GRPO, roughly 10% of activated experts change between $\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}$ and $\pi_{\theta}$ for the same token. The authors claim this makes the token-level ratio $w_{i,t}(\theta) = \frac{ \pi_{\theta} (y_{i,t} | \dots) }{ \pi_{\theta_\text{old}} (y_{i,t} | \dots) }$ fluctuate drastically. Could someone explain the mechanism here? If an expert changes, doesn't the new expert simply output a probability for that token? Why does swapping the underlying network component cause the *ratio* to become unstable or meaningless compared to the dense model case?

questions.title: Is GSPO-token mathematically equivalent to GSPO when advantages are uniform?
questions.question_body: In Section 3.3, the paper introduces GSPO-token with a modified importance weight $s_{i,t}(\theta) = \mathrm{sg}[s_i(\theta)] \cdot \frac{ \pi_{\theta} (y_{i,t}|\dots) }{ \mathrm{sg}[\pi_{\theta} (y_{i,t}|\dots)] }$. The text states this term is numerically equal to 1, making $s_{i,t}$ equal to $s_i$. However, looking at the gradient derivation in Eq. 9, it seems the stop-gradient operations are crucial. If I implement this in PyTorch, does `sg[s_i] * (prob / sg[prob])` truly result in the exact same computational graph and gradient flow as the original GSPO objective when $\widehat{A}_{i,t} = \widehat{A}_{i}$? I am worried I might be missing a subtle difference in how the autograd engine handles the division by a detached value.

questions.title: Why does clipping entire sequences (discarding more data) lead to higher training efficiency?
questions.question_body: Section 4.2 notes a 'curious observation': GSPO clips two orders of magnitude more tokens than GRPO because it discards an entire sequence if *any* part of it falls outside the clip range. Intuitively, throwing away more data should slow down convergence or require more samples. Yet, the paper claims GSPO is *more* efficient. Does this imply that the gradients from the 'partially clipped' sequences in GRPO are actually harmful (high variance noise) rather than just less useful? How does removing these noisy signals accelerate learning enough to offset the loss of sample count?

questions.title: What is the theoretical justification for claiming GRPO's token-level weighting is 'ill-posed'?
questions.question_body: The Motivation section argues that GRPO is ill-posed because importance sampling requires averaging over multiple samples from the behavior distribution to correct distributional mismatch, but GRPO applies weights to single token samples ($N=1$ per position). Standard PPO also uses token-level weights on single samples without collapsing immediately. What is the specific mathematical breakdown that occurs in GRPO's formulation due to this 'single sample' issue that doesn't occur in standard PPO? Is it strictly because GRPO lacks a value function baseline to reduce variance, or is there a fundamental bias introduced by applying sequence-level rewards to token-level weights?

questions.title: How do precision discrepancies between inference and training engines affect likelihood recomputation?
questions.question_body: In Section 4.4, the authors suggest GSPO allows skipping likelihood recomputation on the training engine because sequence-level likelihoods are more tolerant of precision errors between engines (like vLLM vs. Megatron). Since sequence likelihood is just the product of token likelihoods ($ \prod p_t $), wouldn't small precision errors at each token step compound multiplicatively into a massive error for long sequences? Why would the aggregated sequence metric be *more* robust to floating-point differences than checking individual token probabilities?

questions.title: Why are the optimal clipping ranges for GSPO ($3e^{-4}$) so much smaller than for GRPO ($0.2$)?
questions.question_body: The experimental setup specifies clipping ranges of roughly $0.0003$ for GSPO versus $0.2$ for GRPO. Given that both use a min/clip objective structure, why is there such a vast difference in scale? Is this solely because $s_i(\theta)$ is a geometric mean (which stays close to 1) whereas token ratios can vary wildly? If I were to tune GSPO on a new dataset, should I expect these hyperparameters to remain in the $10^{-4}$ range regardless of model size, or does this scale with something else?
